title: Policing Disorder in the AI Era: Historical Contexts and Socialist and Palestine-Solidarity Symbolism in European Protests
content: Public disorder challenges policing capacity, institutional legitimacy, and the protection of peaceful assembly. Drawing on an institutional adaptation framework, this study examines European protests during September–October 2026 alongside historical contexts from France, Russia, and Iran. The study examined approximately 24 hours of publicly available YouTube and online television coverage from France, Italy, Spain, Belgium, and Portugal through iterative thematic analysis and supplementary critical multimodal discourse analysis. Three themes emerged: educational grievances and political symbolism; revolutionary rhetoric and organizational support; and public disorder and police responses. Slogans, flags, and performances connected material concerns with claims about identity and authority. Recordings also documented property destruction, looting, street obstructions, and varied police interventions, including coordinated arrests, tear gas, and water cannons. Peaceful participation and violent conduct coexisted within broader mobilizations, limiting interpretations of uniform intentions or coordinated revolutionary objectives. Findings highlight communication, mobility, operational coordination, and accountability as priorities for institutional preparedness. Historical parallels remain contextual, and the study does not establish that AI caused unrest or that particular technologies would necessarily prevent violence in all circumstances. Emerging capabilities, however, offer hope for predicting, preventing, and mitigating violence, disorder, and looting, but they require independent evaluation and must be used to ensure peaceful assembly.
